title: How to Build a Personalised Assessment System Using Google NotebookLM
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives teachers a ten-step tutorial for using Google NotebookLM to build an assessment system from their own standards and their own definition of mastery. The process runs in three phases: load standards and a spoken interpretation of mastery into the tool, generate performance tasks, performance levels and alternative grading structures, then test and refine against real student work. The central claim is that generic rubrics are written for a hypothetical classroom, whereas a system built from the teacher's own language is defensible and communicates learning to students. NotebookLM is treated as a conversation partner to push back on, with gaps between its output and the teacher's expectations counted as useful data. The later steps use the tool to draft individualized feedback and to track growth across assessment points. The post carries membership and consultancy promotion, but the body is a substantive classroom workflow for a specific AI tool.
points: The workflow starts from the teacher's own messy standards and a recorded description of mastery, so the AI externalizes existing expertise rather than replacing it.
Teachers define their own performance-level labels and grading language, rather than adopting rubric boilerplate that has lost its meaning.
Validating the generated guide against real student samples is a required step, and mismatches are treated as information about vague descriptors.
NotebookLM drafts feedback tied to the performance levels, which the teacher edits, saving time while keeping the teacher's voice.
Reusing the same levels and language across the year turns assessment into a visible story of growth rather than a single percentage.
quotes: Most rubrics weren’t built for your classroom. They were built for a hypothetical one, neat on a grid, that doesn’t account for the unpredictable work students produce when they’re actually engaged. This tutorial walks you through a ten-step process using Google NotebookLM to build an assessment system from your own standards, in your own language, validated against real student work.

That gap, as the image makes clear, tells you something important about your actual expectations. The misses aren’t failures of the tool. They’re data about what you value that never made it into writing.
Traditional rubrics hand you language. “Demonstrates a thorough understanding.” “Limited evidence of...” You’ve read those phrases so many times they’ve lost their meaning.

You might use narrative feedback that describes what students did and what comes next. Skills might be tracked separately from content knowledge. The goal, as the image frames it, is communication: does your grading system help students understand what they can do and what’s next, or does it reduce learning to a number?

Gaps between your system and reality are useful information, not failures. They tell you that descriptions might be too vague, or that your performance tasks aren’t drawing out what you actually want to see. The image makes this point plainly: test early, adjust, and make sure your assessment catches what matters.

A system used repeatedly becomes a story. Apply the same performance levels and language across multiple assessment points throughout the year. A student who started at Emerging in Term 1 and reaches Proficient by Term 3 has a visible learning journey one that a single percentage can never capture.
